Careless tourists are damaging ancient rock art

Thousands of ancient images carved into the rocks of one of France's most popular tourist attractions are being gradually destroyed. Scientists and researchers fear that the 36,000 drawings on the rocks in Mont Bego in the French Alps will be so quickly damaged that they will no longer remain for future generations.
The mountain, which is believed to have once been a place of worship, is covered in drawings that are 4,000 years old, carved into the rough rock. They include images of horned cattle, plowed fields, and various gods and goddesses. But as the popularity of the site increases, the images are being damaged by thoughtless graffiti.
Jean Clottes, chairman of the International Committee for Rock Art, says: 'People think that because the images have been there for so long, they will always be there. But if the damage continues at this rate, there will be nothing left in 50 years.'
He describes how tourists are covering up the drawings, damaging both the rock and the artwork itself. He says that some visitors even take pieces of the rock as souvenirs.
'If people think they can't get a good photo, they will scrape the drawings to get a clearer image,' he says. 'The drawings are also being altered by the weather, and if the sun is shining and the visitors can't see them properly, they will simply scrape them to make them look fresh.'
Other researchers describe how people arrive with long sticks with sharp ends to carve their own drawings, or even their names, into the rocks.
But experts disagree on the best way to preserve the drawings. Henry de Lumley, director of the Natural History Museum in Paris, believes that the only way to save the site is to make the entire mountain a 'no-go' area, allowing access only through guided tours.

The Wrong Country

Uncle chose for them a package holiday at a very reasonable price: a flight from Gatwick Airport, twelve nights in Venice, the fairyland city, in the Pensione Concordia. When Keith and Dawne went together to the travel agency to make the booking, the counter clerk explained that the other members of that particular package were a school group from the south coast, all of them learning Italian. But something went wrong.
Either in the travel agency or at the check-in desk, or in some anonymous computer, a small calamity was conceived. Dawne and Keith ended up in a hotel called the Edelweiss, in Room 212, somewhere in Switzerland.
At Gatwick they had handed their tickets to a girl in the yellow-and-red Your-Kind-of-Holiday uniform. She'd addressed them by name, had checked the details on their tickets and said that that was lovely. An hour later it had surprised them to hear elderly people on the plane talking in North of England accents. Keith said there must have been a cancellation, or possibly the Italian class was on a second plane.
They ordered two drinks, and then two more. 'The coach'll take us on,' a stout woman with spectacles announced when they touched down. 'Keep all together now.' There's been no mention of an overnight stop in the brochure, but when the coach drew in at its destination, Keith explained that that was clearly what this was. As they stepped out of the coach it was close on midnight: fatigued and travel-stained, they did not feel like questioning their right to the beds they were offered.
But the next morning, when it became apparent that they were being offered them for the duration of their holiday, they became alarmed.
'We have the lake, and the water birds,' the receptionist smilingly explained. 'And we may take the steamer to Interlaken.'
'An error has been made,' Keith informed the man, keeping the register of his voice even, for it was essential to be calm. He was aware of his wive's agitated breathing close beside him.
'We were meant to be in Venice. In the Pensione Concordia.'
'I do not know the name, sir. This is Switzerland.'
'A coach is to take us on. An official said so on the plane. She was here last night, that woman.'
'Your group is booked twelve nights in the Edelweiss Hotel. To make an alteration now, sir, if you have changed your minds -'
'We haven't changed our minds. Theres been a mistake.'
The receptionist shook his head. He did not know about a mistake.
'The man who made the booking,' Dawne interrupted, 'was bald, with glasses and a moustache.' She gave the name of the travel agency in London.
'Some problem, have we?' a woman said, beaming at Keith. She was the stout woman he had referred to as an official. They'd seen her talking to the yellow-and-red girl at Gatwick. On the plane she'd walked up and down the aisle, smiling at people.
'My name is Franks,' she was saying now. 'I'm married to the man with the bad leg.'
'Are you in charge, Mrs Franks?' Dawne enquired. 'Only we're in the wrong hotel.'
Again she gave the name of the travel agency and described the bald-headed counter clerk, mentioning his spectacles and his moustache. Keith interrupted her. 'It seems we got into the wrong group. We reported to the Your-Kind-of-Holiday girl and left it all to her.'
'We should have known when they weren't from Dover,' Dawne contributed. 'We heard them talking about Darlington.'
Keith made an impatient sound. He wished sh'ed leave the talking to him.
'We noticed you at Gatwick,' Keith said. 'We knew you were in charge of things.'
'And I noticed you. I counted you, although I daresay you didn't see me doing that. Now, let me explain to you. There are many places Your-Kind-of-Holiday sends its clients to, many different holidays at different prices. There are, for instance, villa holidays for the adventurous under-thirty-fives. There are treks to Turkey, and treks for singles to the Himalayas.'
'Now, what I am endeavouring to say to you good people is that all tickets and labels are naturally similar, the yellow with the two red bands.' Mrs Franks suddenly laughed. 'So if you simply followed other people with the yellow-and-red label you might imagine you could end up in a wildlife park! But of course,' she added soothingly, 'that couldn't happen in a million years.'
'We're not meant to be in Switzerland,' Keith doggedly persisted.
'Well, let's just see, shall we?'
Unexpectediy, Mrs Franks turned and went away, leaving them standing. The receptionist was no longer behind the reception desk. The sound of typing could be heard.
'She seems quite kind,' Dawne whispered, 'that woman.' Keith wasn't listening. He tried to go over in his mind every single thing that had occurred: handing the girl the tickets, sitting down to wait, and then the girl leading the way to the plane, and then the pilot's voice welcoming them aboard, and the air hostess with the smooth black hair going round to see that everyone's seat belt was fastened.
'Nice to have some young people along,' an elderly man's voice interrupted Keith's thoughts. 'Nottage the name is.' The old man's wife was with him, both of them looking as if they were in their eighties. They'd slept like logs, she said, best night's sleep they'd had for years, which of course would be due to the lakeside air.
'Thats nice,' Dawne said.
Keith walked out of the reception area and Dawne followed him. On the forecourt of the hotel they didn't say to one another that there was an irony in the catastrophe that had occurred. On their first holiday since their honeymoon they'd landed themselves in a package tour of elderly people when the whole point of the holiday was to escape the needs and demands of the elderly. In his bossy way Uncle had said so himself when they'd tried to persuade him to accompany them.

results.src_text:
The camera never lies 

Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of the Sherlock Holmes stories, believed himself to be a rational man, a scientist even. But in 1920, when he saw photographs of fairies taken in a garden setting, he thought he was seeing scientific proof that these tiny creatures really existed. He published the photographs alongside an article he wrote, acknowledging fairies as supernatural wonders. It was not until 1939 that the two ladies who took the photos admitted these were fake. They simply cut out pictures of fairies from a book and arranged them among flowers. The results are undeniably beautiful. But the simplicity of the trick undermines a basic principle of photography, that the camera cannot lie. 
But it can, and always could. Today, we are used to computer software enabling us to rework our digital images and it is a myth that photography ever had a true age of innocence. From the moment cameras began capturing reality, that reality was being altered.

Art

In modern times - more and more over the course of the last two hundred years - we have come to speak as though every artist had to rebel against the art of his contemporaries. Art is praised in terms of being unique, revolutionary, shocking even. We feel good about admiring the artist whose work no one appreciated a hundred years ago. But when we get to the art of our own day, we get cold feet and say that an artist has gone too far, that what he does can no longer be called art. Or, rather, the media say it for us. And, on the whole, we agree because we expect to be puzzled by art's insistent newness - so much so that we do not notice the old themes, methods and also virtues that the art of our own time is full of.
We require artists to be separate from the rest of us, figures with special talents and drive, so vigorous that conventions cannot contain them. Previous ages went to artists with commissions: people needed art for specific purposes, and it was part of their ordinary life. Today we leave artists to their own devices and get rather cross with them if they want to come down out of the clouds.

Picture This

I am going to describe a situation, and then ask a crucial question about it. I hope it doesn't strike you as unduly gnomic. But if it does, that's modern art for you.
Here's the situation. An artist chooses a piece of text in an art book. The text considers the diversity of pictures. 'What are they all about?' it asks dumbly, before deciding, even more dumbly: 'There is no end, in fact, to the number of different kinds of pictures.' Okay, this is kiddy-language, and so far all it has betrayed is kiddy-thinking. But stick with me, all you adults out there. The situation is about to complicate itself.
Having settled on his text, the man then asks someone else to make a canvas for him, to stretch it and prime it, and then to take it along to a sign painter. He asks the sign painter to write the chosen text on the canvas. And he gives the sign painter specific instructions not to attempt anything flashy or charming with the lettering. The sign painter does all this. On a white canvas, in simple black letters, he writes the chosen text. So my crucial question is this: is the finished product a painting?

Underground Encounters

At the Mercury Gallery, London until 26th June

It is an unspoken rule of commercial success as a painter that once you have developed a profitable line in one genre, you stick to it. Collectors expect an artist to diligently mine the same seam, and attempts to strike out in a new direction are usually met at best with indignation and the feeling that the artist has let the public down.
Why this should be I'm not entirely sure. Gallery owners obviously prefer safe bets, and perhaps the art-buying public is insecure and needs the comfort of continuity. A few artists break the mould and get away with it. Picasso and Hockney are two prime examples. Eric Rimmington is another artist who is now gamely running contrary to form, and it remains to be seen if he can pull it off. His new show takes the daring step of swapping the pristine still lifes which have made his name for paintings of the world of the London Underground.
Railways hold a peculiar charm for Rimmington. From drawings made in the 1980s of the railway land of Londons Kings Cross Station, it was a logical step to go beneath the ground and look at what was happening below. The sketches have provided the material for Underground Encounters, an exhibition of 40 paintings and drawings which convey the curious magic of this sunken world designed for a population in transit.

Extract from a novel

I have escaped to this island with a few books. I do not know why I use the word 'escape'. The villagers say jokingly that only a sick man would choose such a remote place to rebuild. Well then, I have come here to heal myself, if you like to put it that way.
Apart from the wrinkled old peasant who comes from the village on her mule each day to clean the house, I am quite alone. I am neither happy nor unhappy; I lie suspended like a hair or a feather in the cloudy mixtures of memory. I spoke of the uselessness of art but added nothing truthful about its consolations. The solace of such work as I do with brain and heart lies in this - that only there, in the silences of the painter or the writer can reality be reordered, reworked and made to show its significant side. Our common actions in reality are simply the sackcloth covering which hides the cloth-of-gold - the meaning of the pattern. For us artists there waits the joyous compromise through art with all that wounded or defeated us in daily life; in this way, not to evade destiny, as the ordinary people try to do, but to fulfil it in its true potential - the imagination. Otherwise why should we hurt one another?

results.src_text:
THE HISTORY OF THE IDITAROD - THE LAST GREAT RACE ON EARTH

In the 1880s, gold was discovered in what is now the most northern state of the USA,
Alaska. Many people came to the area hoping to get rich. New towns were built and grew quickly. One such town was called Iditarod, which means 'far, distant place'. This town grew so quickly during 1909 that it briefly became the largest city in Alaska. In the summer months, essential supplies could be delivered to these towns by boat, but in the winter the rivers and the ocean froze and there was no way to get to them. So, in 1910, a winter track was built which would be used by teams of dogs pulling sleds. They would take mail, food and clothes to the gold miners.
The track became known as the Iditarod Trail. It took a team of dogs about three weeks to travel across Alaska. They stopped at 'roadhouses' where the drivers could get a warm bed for the night and something to eat for both themselves and their dogs. The trail was used every winter until the 1920s when aeroplanes replaced steam boats and dog teams as the main form of transport.
However, the dogs had one last taste of fame in 1925, when a disease called diphtheria hit the city of Nome. The disease could be cured, but, unfortunately, the closest medicine that could be found was in Anchorage, right on the other side of Alaska. Aeroplanes were still quite new, so no-one knew if they could fly in such cold weather. Also, Carl Eielson, the only pilot considered skilled enough to manage the flight, was away on a trip at the time. It was therefore agreed that the medicine would be transported using teams of dogs instead.
The trip covered over 1,000 kilometres, most of it along the Iditarod Trail. It took twenty teams just six days to complete the journey. Leonhard Seppala, a Norwegian who had come to Alaska looking for gold, travelled the first 400 of those kilometres. He had to trust his dog Togo's ability to find his way in the blinding snow and Togo turned out to be a reliable guide. The last part of the journey was done by Gunnar Kaasen who had driven dog teams in Alaska for 21 years. His lead dog was Saito. At one point Balto refused to go any further, and saved the team from falling into icy water. The diphtheria was stopped and Balto became a hero.
Nowadays a dog sled race is held every year from Anchorage to Nome, following the route of that famous journey in 1925. It is called the Iditarod and has become known as 'The Last Great Race on Earth'.

We changed lives for a day!

Have you ever dreamed about swapping lives with someone else for a day? Perhaps you think it would be more fun to do something quite different for a change? We fixed it for four people - read how it went.
Amanda (23), a young mother with two daughters, swapped lives with her friend Cindy (30), who works as a waitress at a glitzy London restaurant and entertainment complex.

A. Amanda's story

I'd never been inside anywhere remotely like it before. I couldn't believe how dark and noisy it was - there were so many people and such a brilliant atmosphere. It was all a far cry from my home town and, to he honest, I wasn't sure I'd survive! Being a mother is definitely a busy job - but this was something else!
I had just fifteen minutes to learn how to carry a tray of drinks at shoulder height with one hand. The other waitresses made it look so simple, but just as I was getting the hang of it, the drinks started to slide off the tray and crashed on to the floor, splattering cocktails everywhere. I was so embarrassed, but all the other waitresses laughed. Everyone makes a fool of themselves at first!
By opening time at 11.30 am, a queue had already formed outside and I began to feel really nervous. I was worried about how I'd remember all the orders, but that, at least, wasn't a problem because everything was automated.
After a couple of hours my feet really ached and I couldn't get used to the constant loud music. Every time a customer spoke to me I had to say 'Pardon?', which was so embarrassing! By the end of my shift at 5 pm, I was totally exhausted and longed to soak my feet in a bowl of hot water. I couldn't believe it when one of the waitresses told me it had been a 'quiet' day!
I never realised how tiring waitressing would be. I've always thought it was a job for shrinking violets, but in fact you definitely need to be quite bubbly, as well having the ability to keep a cool head and deal with what is known in the trade as a 'high-volume experience' - in other words, lots of customers!
I'm really quite shy and I don't think I could cope on a Saturday night, when it gets chaotically busy. I wasn't too impressed with the pay either. Unfortunately, I must have been a lousy waitress because even the rich Americans didn't tip me a bean!
I must admit I was very glad to get back to my children. It seems quite easy after waitressing!

B. Cindy's story

I was feeling quite apprehensive about being a 'mum' for the day, but I was looking forward to it, too. I'd been warned the girls were cheeky, but in my ignorance I thought I could handle it. Little did I know!
As Amanda left to make her way to the restaurant, I had to get the two girls dressed and fed. After dropping off Sophie at school and Katie at nursery I thought I'd have three hours of peace. Wrong! A note from Amanda reminded me that I still had to make the beds, clean the house and do the washing.
At 1 pm I picked up Katie, whizzed around the supermarket and then took her home for lunch. But it was when I brought Sophie home from school that the real trouble started. They turned the settee into a trampoline and played a game which involved screaming as loudly as they possibly could! I decided to take the laid-back approach, imagining they'd soon get worn out. Wrong again. I thought I had a fair amount of stamina, but they beat me, hands down!
After much persuasion, I managed to get them into bed by about 8 pm, but then the fun and games started! How many glasses of water can a child drink, for heaven's sake? Of course, I realised it was just a ploy so they could come downstairs and watch television, but it was exhausting to spend all evening negotiating deals with them.
I never realised how tiring it could be looking after two small children. You don't get a second to think about yourself - and the sheer sense of responsibility is overwhelming. Even so, I really enjoyed the day.

Rosemary (42) runs a dairy farm. She swapped with Hilary (30), a teacher at a primary school.

C. Rosemary's story

On the farm, I have to get up at 5.30 am so sleeping in until 7 was pure luxury! But I dithered for ages about how to look. I could hardly turn up in overalls and boots, could I?
Looking at a sea of faces -- about 400 pupils -- at assembly, I hoped I melted into the background and that my fresh complexion didn't make me stand out as being straight off the farm.
After that it was time for a maths class. The children worked in small groups, using workcards graded according to difficulty - rather different from when I was at school and we had to recite tables in unison! Then I helped out with a nature project - identifying and feeding species of snails.
By lunchtime I was exhausted and looking forward to an hour's break, but the teachers only have about five minutes to eat their meal. There's so much to do before classes start again. I attended a staff meeting about reports and couldn't avoid getting roped in to help with athletics trials.
Alter lunch there was a silent reading lesson (bliss!) and then a French lesson in the video room. This was great fun because all the children wanted to practise on me, which really showed up my rusty French.
Finally we moved on to the school hall for Physical Education. I was drained by now, but the children seemed to have inexhaustible energy.
The hardest part of the job was standing up in front of the class and speaking - even for just two minutes, it's daunting. Teachers may get more holidays a year, but I think I'll stick to farming, anyway!

D. Hilary's story

I arrived at White House Farm at 8.30 am, bright and early, only to discover that Rosemary had been up for three hours! Rosemary's 280-acre farm has 100 Jersey cows, 15 calves and heifers and about 800 ewes! As well as milk, she manufactures ice-cream, yoghurt and cream, which is sold in shops, restaurants and at tourist attractions. I spent most of the morning in the ice-cream parlour, bottling milk into plastic litre containers, squeezing ice-cream from a machine into cartons and sticking on labels. It was difficult to stop myself dipping my fingers into the goodies! At lunchtime it was time to inspect the sheep. I drove over to one of the fields and picked up a ewe which had fallen over. If the sheep are left for more than 12 hours once they have fallen over they could die, so they have to he checked every day. What a nightmare it must be in winter!
Alter feeding the calves, I started the milking. The process took an exhausting two-and-a-half hours. And Rosemary does this twice a day, starting at 6 am, seven days a week, 365 days a year!
I found it quite a lonely day. I was surprised how much I missed the children - animals don't answer back! The worst aspect of the job is not being able to get away from work. The cows always have to be milked twice a day, so it's really difficult to plan any time off. Rosemary will only get about three days' holiday this year.
Farming seems romantic but the reality is very different. The income is irregular and I'd hate to be at the mercy of the weather.

Little Chefs

For one group of children aged between ten and fifteen, Saturdays are spent learning the art of serious cooking. Their weekly lessons in small classes are so popular that there is a waiting list of 30 children who want to do the course. Parents pay PS280 for the course where their children can have fun and learn how to make good food.
Class member Bill, aged ten, says, 'I love my mum's cooking and now I can do it better than her. The teachers make us laugh, especially when we sit down with them to share the food we've made.'
Flora is twelve, and she's having problems preparing onions. 'I love cooking. I did a meal for ten friends which they really enjoyed. Then my mum suggested I take up a hobby, instead of doing nothing at weekends. I was happy staying at home, so I wasn't too keen at first. I'm really glad I decided to come, though.'
Their teacher, Philippe, says, 'It's great fun. Children pay attention and remember things better than adults, although the kitchen isn't always as tidy when they're cooking! As adults, we're always learning more about food. If parents interest their children in cooking while they are young, they'll have enough skill to make food for themselves when they leave home.'

CARTOON FILMS 

Cartoon films have very few limits. If you can draw something, you can make it move on the cinema screen. The use of new ideas and advanced computer programs means that cartoons are becoming exciting again for people of all ages. 
By the end of the 1970s, the cinema world had decided that cartoons were only for children. 
But soon afterwards, one or two directors had some original new ideas. They proved that it was possible to make films in which both adults and children could share the fun. 
However, not every cartoon film was successful. The Black Cauldron, for example, failed, mainly because it was too frightening for children and too childish for adults. Directors learnt from this mistake, and the film companies began to make large amounts of money again.

Simon Costello knew that the purchase of the house in Pembroke Square had been a mistake within a year of his and Lois's moving in. A possession which can only be afforded by the exercise of stringent and calculated economy is best not afforded at all. But at the time it had seemed a sensible, as well as a desirable, move. He had had a run of successful cases and they were coming in with reassuring regularity. Lois had returned to her job at the advertising agency within two months of the birth of the twins, and had been given a rise which took her salary to thirty-five thousand. It was Lois who had argued the more strongly for a move, but he had put up little resistance to arguments which at the time had seemed compelling: the flat wasn't really suitable for a family, they needed more room, a garden, separate accommodation for an au pair. All these, of course, could have been achieved in a suburb or in a less fashionable part of London than Pembroke Square, but Lois was ambitious for more than additional space. Mornington Mansions had never been an acceptable address for an up-and-coming young barrister and a successful businesswoman. She never said it without a sense that even speaking the words subtly diminished her standing, socially and economically.
Lois had decided that a necessary economy was for one of them to travel by public transport. Her firm was on the other side of London; obviously Simon must be the one to economise. The overcrowded tube journey, stayed in a mood of envious resentment, had become an unproductive thirty minutes of brooding on present discontents. He would recall his grandfather's house in Hampstead where he had stayed as a boy, the smell of dinner from the kitchen, his grandmother's insistence that the returning breadwinner, tired from his exhausting day in court, should be given peace, a little gentle cosseting, and relief from every petty domestic anxiety. She had been a 'lawyer's wife', indefatigable in legal good causes, elegantly present at all lawyers' functions, apparently content with the sphere of life which she had made her own. Well, that world had passed for ever. Lois had made it plain before their marriage that her career was as important as his. It hardly needed saying, this was, after all, a modern marriage. The job was important to her and important to them both. The house, the au pair, their whole standard of living depended on two salaries. And now what they were precariously achieving could be destroyed by that self-righteous, interfering Venetia.
Venetia must have come straight from the court to their offices and she had been in a dangerous mood. Something or someone had upset her. But the word 'upset' was too weak, too bland for the intensity of furious disgust with which she had confronted him. Someone had driven her to the limit of her endurance. He cursed himself. If he hadn't been in his room, if he'd only left a minute earlier, the encounter wouldn't have taken place, she would have had the night to think it over, to consider what, if anything, she ought to do. Probably nothing. The morning might have brought sense. He remembered every word of her angry accusations.
'I defended Brian Cartwright today. Successfully. He told me that when you were his counsel four years ago you knew before trial that he had bribed three of the jury. You did nothing. You went on with the case. Is that true?'
'He's lying. It isn't true.'
'He also said that he passed over some shares in his company to your fiancee. Also before trial. Is that true?'
'I tell you, he's lying. None of its true.'
The denial had been as instinctive as an arm raised to ward off a blow and had sounded unconvincing even to his own ears. His whole action had been one of guilt. The first cold horror draining his face was succeeded by a hot flush, bringing back shameful memories of his headmaster's study, of the terror of the inevitable punishment. He had made himself look into her eyes and had seen the look of contemptuous disbelief. If only he'd had some warning. He knew now what he should have said: 'Cartwright told me after the trial but I didn't believe him. I don't believe him now. That man will say anything to make himself important.'
But he had told a more direct, more dangerous lie, and she had known that it was a lie. Even so, why the anger, why the disgust? What was that old misdemeanour to do with her? Who had sent Venetia Aldridge to be guardian of the conscience of their legal practice? Or of his, come to that? Was her own conscience so clear, her behaviour in court always immaculate? Was she justified in destroying his career? And it would be destruction. He wasn't sure what exactly she could do, how far she was prepared to go, but if this got about, even as a rumour, he was done for.

A trumpet isn't just for Christmas...

It is strange how many musicians, even leading ones, come from homes without music. Out of the blue, Hakan Hardenberger, the only son of totally unmusical parents in a country district of southern Sweden, has at the age of 30 established himself as unique among the world's trumpet-players today.
His records are continually opening up new repertory, not just concertos by long-neglected composers of the baroque and classical periods, but new works too. When you meet him, bright-eyed and good-looking, he seems even younger than his years, as fresh and open in his manner as the sound of the trumpet.
Recently in one of London's premier concert halls he played the Hummel Trumpet Concerto, something of a party-piece for him, while on television a whole feature was devoted to his work and development, filmed both here and in Sweden.
Born near Malmo, he owes his career to the accident of a Christmas present when he was only eight.
His father, unmusical but liking Louis Armstrong's playing, had the idea of giving his only son a trumpet. Being a serious man, he didn't pick a toy trumpet, but took advice and bought a genuine grown-up instrument.
The success of the gift was instant. The boy never stopped playing. His mother managed to contact the second trumpet-player in the Malmo Symphony Orchestra, whom she persuaded to give her son lessons.
Bo Nilsson was an up-and-coming musician, and at once spotted natural talent. Hardenberger consistently blesses his luck to have got such a teacher right from the start, one who was himself so obsessed with the trumpet and trumpet-playing that he would search out and contact players all over the world, and as a 'trumpet fanatic' was 'always looking for another mouthpiece'.
There the mature Hardenberger has to draw a line between himself and his teacher. 'The trumpet is so primitive an instrument,' he explains, 'that you can't build a trumpet that is acoustically perfect. Whatever you do, it will have imperfections. Besides, you can't find two mouthpieces exactly the same. To me it is a matter of getting to know the imperfections and making a relationship with them.'
From the very start Hardenberger seems to have had the gift of finding the right compromise, and making that relationship. Without any sense of boasting, he explains that even in his boyhood years the characteristic Hardenberger sound was already recognisable, 'the first thing I acquired'.
And unlike the great British contender among virtuoso trumpet-players, John Wallace, who developed originally from a brass-band background and then through working in orchestras, Hardenberger has always thought of himself as a solo artist pure and simple.
From early boyhood he had as a role-model the French trumpeter, Maurice Andre, another player who bypassed the orchestra. The boy bought all his records, and idolised him.
His parents gave him every chance to practise, and went along with his ambition to make trumpet-playing a career. It was then a question of where, at 15, he should be sent to study. America, Bo Nilsson's first choice, was thought to be too far away and too dangerous, which meant that he went instead at the age of 16 to study in Paris with Pierre Thibaud. Thibaud confirmed his prejudice against going into an orchestra, saying that 'Playing in the orchestra is like digging in the garden.'
He was objective enough about himself to know that he played the trumpet better than others of his age, but it was only at the end of the first competition he entered, at the age of 17 during his first year in Paris, that he came to realise that in addition he had a particular gift of communicating.
Thibaud suggested that he should enter the competition just for experience. Hardenberger learned the pieces for the first round only, but he won through to the second. Luckily he already knew most of the pieces in that round too, but on getting through to the final he was faced with a concerto that had already daunted him. He didn't win first prize that time, but he enjoyed the performance, realising that though he 'played like a pig', people did listen to him.
Quoted like that, Hardenberger's realism about his work and his career may sound arrogant, but that would be a totally false impression. Thoughtfully he refuses to try and analyse what such a gift of communication might consist of, as 'You risk destroying it in trying to explain. The power of the music lies in the fact that it can always move people.'
results.tgt_text:
Een trompet is niet alleen voor kerst...

Het is opvallend hoeveel musici, zelfs de meest bekende, afkomstig zijn uit gezinnen zonder muzikale traditie. Hakan Hardenberger, de enige zoon van volledig onmuzikale ouders in een landelijk gebied in het zuiden van Zweden, heeft op 30-jarige leeftijd een unieke positie verworven onder de trompetspelers ter wereld.
Zijn opnames onthullen voortdurend nieuwe repertoire, niet alleen concerten van vergeten componisten uit de barok- en klassieke periode, maar ook nieuwe werken. Wanneer je hem ontmoet, met heldere ogen en een aantrekkelijke uitstraling, lijkt hij nog jonger dan zijn leeftijd, net zo fris en open als het geluid van de trompet.
Recente optredens in een van de belangrijkste concertzalen van Londen omvatten bijvoorbeeld de Hummel-trompetconcerto, een stuk dat hij met veel plezier speelt. Op televisie werd een volledig programma gewijd aan zijn werk en ontwikkeling, gefilmd zowel in Londen als in Zweden.
Geboren in de buurt van Malmo, is zijn carrière te danken aan een toevallige gebeurtenis tijdens de kerst, toen hij nog maar acht jaar oud was.
Zijn vader, die geen muzikale achtergrond had, maar wel bewondering had voor het spel van Louis Armstrong, besloot zijn enige zoon een trompet te geven. Hij koos niet voor een speelgoedtrompet, maar nam advies in en kocht een echte, volwassen instrument.
Het succes was onmiddellijk. De jongen stopte nooit met spelen. Zijn moeder wist de tweede trompetspeler in het Malmo Symfonieorkest te bereiken, en overtuigde hem om zijn zoon les te geven.
Bo Nilsson was een opkomende muzikant, en herkende meteen het natuurlijke talent van Hardenberger. Hardenberger is altijd dankbaar voor de kans die hij kreeg om zo vroeg in zijn leven een dergelijke leraar te hebben, iemand die zelf zo gepassioneerd was over de trompet en het trompetspelen dat hij contact maakte met spelers over de hele wereld. Hij beschouwt zichzelf als een 'trompetfanatic', die altijd op zoek is naar een nieuwe 'mouthpiece'.
Hardenberger zelf moet nu een grens trek
results.back_text:
A trumpet is not just for Christmas...

It's remarkable how many musicians, even the most famous, come from families without a musical tradition. Hakan Hardenberger, the only son of completely non-musical parents in a rural area in southern Sweden, has achieved a unique position among trumpet players worldwide at the age of 30.
His recordings consistently reveal new repertoire, not only concertos by forgotten composers from the Baroque and Classical periods, but also new works. When you meet him, with clear eyes and an attractive appearance, he seems younger than his age, just as fresh and open as the sound of the trumpet.
Recent performances in one of London's most prestigious concert halls have included the Hummel trumpet concerto, a piece that he plays with great enjoyment. A full program dedicated to his work and development was also broadcast on television, filmed both in London and in Sweden.
Born near Malmo, his career began as a result of a chance event during Christmas, when he was only eight years old.
His father, who had no musical background but admired the playing of Louis Armstrong, decided to give his only son a trumpet. He didn't choose a toy trumpet, but sought advice and bought a real, adult instrument.
The success was immediate. The boy never stopped playing. His mother managed to contact the second trumpet player in the Malmo Symphony Orchestra and persuaded him to give his son lessons.
Bo Nilsson was an up-and-coming musician who immediately recognized Hardenberger's natural talent. Hardenberger has always been grateful for the opportunity to have such a teacher so early in his life, someone who was so passionate about the trumpet and playing that he made contact with players all over the world. He considers himself a "trumpet fanatic," always searching for a new "mouthpiece."

results.title: 58.txt
results.src_text:
The Actor's Craft

Derision and contempt are sprayed at actors from time to time. Much of this disdain is fuelled by the actors themselves when they're compelled by their film/theatre companies to talk about their craft (and themselves) in interviews. They should give the dancer Pavlova's reply to the man who asked her what she meant when she was dancing: 'If I could tell you,' she said, 'I wouldn't dance it.' But instead they all too easily fall into ponderous cliches, silly truisms or into the prurient jaws of the gossip machine. We should all pay heed to what Paul Scofield said in a letter to a friend of mine: 'I have found that an actor's work has life and interest only in its execution. It seems to wither away in discussion and become emptily theoretical and insubstantial. It has no rules (except perhaps audibility). With every play and every playwright the actor starts from scratch, as if he or she knows nothing and proceeds to learn afresh every time growing with the relationships of the characters and the insights of the writer. When the play has finished its run, he's empty until the next time. And its the emptiness which is, I find, apparent in any discussion of theatre work.'

A review of Hamlet

Adrian Lester's Hamlet is poised precariously between boyhood and manhood, and it is a performance of thrilling simplicity and assurance. His handling of the text and his physical and psychological self-control take him, in one leap, from brilliantly promising to frontline player: an actor with the intelligent confidence to be almost self-effacing. Lester plays an edgy, tetchy young man who feeds on a banked-down sense of anger, agile, watchful and driven, he deploys a sense of acid wit and generous humour that makes him both formidable and lovable. Although played down, the virtuosity of this performance is unmistakable. Observe Lester's body, the way his arms hang stiffly, giving you a sense of a figure waiting to be animated. Handy's portrayal of Horatio gives you a similar feeling of a body being moved by an inner force that he both knows and does not know. So what is acting? What is behaviour? Is the former an imitation or an evocation of the latter? Who and what animates these bodies, morally and physically? That is the central question about the life of the theatre.

One director's approach to rehearsal

The first stage of this director's rehearsal process is known as 'dropping in', a procedure which goes something like this. The stage manager projects the script onto a screen. The actors sit quietly while someone else is speaking, finding out what effect the words are having. When if is their turn to speak, they glance of the screen, digest the first phrase, think about what it means to them, wait to find the impulse - the reason to speak - then speak. For example, the line is, 'Queuing all night, the rain, do you remember?; Breathe. Let the thought drop in with your breath. A memory, a vision, an impression. Some people will imagine a queue, maybe at a bus stop on the way to rehearsals or for a rock concert in their youth. Having visualised the scene, find the impulse to speak it - what this director calls 'The pathway to the line'. Impulses can come from without or within. Look in the eyes of the other actor listening. Consider your character's situation. This director talks of 'dropping in' as a means of finding out what is going on. Don't pre-plan or pre-judge. Dare to go down there with an empty mind and trust that something will happen to you.

The Perfect Theatre

The perfect theatre should make you feel as if your presence has made a difference. Going to the theatre, going to any live performance, is an event and the staff need to have a sense of that, too. It's terribly alienating if you feel that its just any old job for the people working front of house.
The theatre itself needs to create a relationship between the performer and the audience - no one in the audience should feel that they're getting an unreasonably prejudiced view of the actor. It's important that they're not too far away, they can hear, they can see, they can feel in some sense in contact with what's going on on stage. The proportions of an auditorium are important. They have to respond to the human voice and the scale of the human body. If an auditorium dwarfs the human body, there's something wrong with it because you can't deny the human form at the heart of drama. A lot of theatres in the late nineteenth century got it right because they managed to shape an auditorium that somehow embraces the stage.
I like theatres that have a sense of the past in them. Like worn stone steps in a church, you get the sense of layers of human presence. From the point of view of the plays, you can't have something for everybody. You cant second-guess an audience because they don't know what they're going to want to see. When you visit the theatre, you want something done in a way you can't imagine, otherwise you may as well have stayed at home.

De kunst van het acteren

Soms worden acteurs bekritiseerd en vernederd. Een groot deel van deze minachting komt van de acteurs zelf, wanneer ze door hun film- of theaterbedrijven worden gevraagd om over hun vak en zichzelf te praten in interviews. Ze zouden Pavlova's antwoord aan de man moeten geven die haar vroeg wat ze bedoelde toen ze danste: "Als ik dat kon vertellen, zou ik het niet meer doen." Maar in plaats daarvan vallen ze vaak te gemakkelijk in oppervlakkige clichés, onzinnige waarheden of in de nieuwsgierige wereld van roddels. We zouden allemaal moeten letten op wat Paul Scofield in een brief aan een vriend van mij schreef: "Ik heb ontdekt dat het werk van een acteur alleen in de uitvoering leven en interesse heeft. Het lijkt te vervallen in discussie en wordt leeg en theoretisch. Het heeft geen regels (behalve misschien de audibiliteit). Bij elke voorstelling en elke schrijver begint de acteur opnieuw, alsof hij of zij niets weet, en leert hij of zij steeds opnieuw, terwijl hij of zij zich ontwikkelt door de relaties tussen de personages en de inzichten van de schrijver."

Een recensie van Hamlet

Adrian Lester's vertolking van Hamlet is precair tussen kindertijd en volwassenheid, en het is een vertolking van opwindende eenvoud en zekerheid. Zijn beheersing van de tekst en zijn fysieke en psychologische zelfbeheersing brengen hem in één keer van een veelbelovende acteur naar een hoofdrolspeler. Lester speelt een nerveuze, geïrriteerde jonge man die leeft van een onderdrukte woede, hij is behendig, alert en gedreven, en hij gebruikt een gevoel van scherpe humor en genereus gevoel, waardoor hij zowel imposant als lieflijk is. Hoewel de vertolking wordt afgezwakt, is de virtuositeit van deze vertolking onmiskenbaar. Let op Lester's lichaam, de manier waarop zijn armen stijf hangen, waardoor je een beeld krijgt van iemand die wacht om tot leven te worden gebracht. results.back_text:
The Art of Acting

Actors are sometimes criticized and belittled. A significant portion of this disdain comes from the actors themselves, when they are asked by their film or theater companies to talk about their profession and themselves in interviews. They should emulate Pavlova's response to the man who asked her what she meant when she danced: "If I could tell you, I wouldn't do it anymore." But instead, they often fall into superficial clichés, nonsensical truths, or the gossipy world of rumors. We should all pay attention to what Paul Scofield wrote in a letter to a friend of mine: "I have discovered that the work of an actor only has life and interest in performance. It seems to degenerate into discussion and becomes empty and theoretical. It has no rules (except perhaps audibility). At every performance and with every writer, the actor starts anew, as if he or she knows nothing, and learns again and again, while developing through the relationships between the characters and the insights of the writer."

A Review of Hamlet

Adrian Lester's portrayal of Hamlet is precariously balanced between childhood and adulthood, and it is a performance of exciting simplicity and certainty. His mastery of the text and his physical and psychological control bring him from a promising actor to a leading role in a single performance. Lester plays a nervous, irritable young man who lives on suppressed anger, he is agile, alert, and driven, and he uses a sense of sharp humor and generous feeling, making him both imposing and endearing. Although the performance is weakened, the virtuosity of this portrayal is undeniable. Pay attention to Lester's body, the way his arms hang stiffly, giving you the impression of someone waiting to be brought to life. Handy's portrayal of Horatio gives you a similar feeling of a body driven by an inner force that he both knows and doesn't know. What is acting?

results.title: La Chandeleur
results.src_text:
Histoire de la Chandeleur 

Bonjour ! Le 2 février, c'est la Chandeleur, l'occasion pour tous les gourmands de manger des crêpes. Mais d'où vient cette tradition de manger des crêpes le 2 février ?  

Eh bien, comme souvent en France, il faut chercher les origines de cette fête à la fois dans des sources païennes et religieuses.  

Chez les Romains, on fêtait les Lupercales aux environs du 15 février, fêtes inspirées de Lupercus, dieu de la fécondité et des troupeaux. Chez les Celtes, on fêtait Imbolc le 1er février. Ce rite, en l'honneur de la déesse Brigit, célébrait la purification et la fertilité au sortir de l'hiver. Les paysans portaient des flambeaux et parcouraient les champs en procession, priant la déesse de purifier la terre avant les semailles.  

Ces traditions païennes ont très longtemps perduré en France, sous la forme de la festa candelarum ce qui signifie en latin « fête des chandelles », ou la Chandeleur, la coutume consistant à allumer des cierges à minuit en symbole de purification.  

Au Ve siècle, le Pape Gélase 1er décide d'associer ces traditions païennes à un événement biblique afin de les transformer en fête chrétienne. Il décide que l'on célèbrera désormais à cette date la Présentation de l'enfant Jésus au Temple de Jérusalem et la purification (ou les relevailles) de sa mère, la sainte Vierge. Dans les églises, on remplace les torches par des chandelles bénites dont la lueur éloigne le Mal et rappelle que le Christ est la lumière du monde. Les chrétiens rapportent ensuite les cierges chez eux afin de protéger leur foyer. Cette fête s'appelle officiellement Présentation du Christ au Temple mais a conservé son nom d'usage d'origine païenne : la Chandeleur.  

« Mais alors » me direz-vous, « et les crêpes dans tout ça ? » Eh bien, c'est à cette époque de l'année que les semailles d'hiver commençaient. Alors, on se servait de la farine que l'on avait fait [sic: should be faite] avec le blé excédentaire pour confectionner des crêpes, symbole de prospérité pour l'année à venir. De plus, les crêpes, par leur forme ronde et dorée, rappellent le disque solaire, évoquant le retour du printemps après l'hiver sombre et froid. On raconte également que ce même pape Gélase Ier faisait distribuer des crêpes aux pèlerins qui arrivaient à Rome.  

Et si cette vidéo vous a donné faim, il ne vous reste plus qu'à vous entraîner à la confection des crêpes, grâce aux vidéos pratiques bien sûr.
results.tgt_text:
The History of Candlemas

Hello! February 2nd is Candlemas, a day when everyone can enjoy eating crêpes. But where does this tradition of eating crêpes on February 2nd come from?

As is often the case in France, the origins of this holiday can be traced to both pagan and religious sources.

The Romans celebrated Lupercalia around February 15th, a festival inspired by Lupercus, the god of fertility and livestock. The Celts celebrated Imbolc on February 1st. This rite, in honor of the goddess Brigit, celebrated purification and fertility at the end of winter. Farmers carried torches and paraded through the fields, praying to the goddess to purify the land before planting.

These pagan traditions persisted for a long time in France, taking the form of "festa candelarum," which means "festival of candles" in Latin, or Candlemas, the custom of lighting candles at midnight as a symbol of purification.

In the 5th century, Pope Gelasius I decided to associate these pagan traditions with a biblical event in order to transform them into a Christian holiday. He decided that this date would now be celebrated with the Presentation of Jesus in the Temple of Jerusalem and the purification (or cleansing) of Mary, the Virgin. In churches, torches were replaced by blessed candles, whose light drove away evil and reminded people that Christ is the light of the world. Christians then took the candles home to protect their homes. This holiday is officially called the Presentation of Christ, but it has retained its original pagan name: Candlemas.

"So," you might ask, "and what about the crêpes?" Well, this is the time of year when winter crops were sown. Therefore, people would use the flour made from surplus wheat to make crêpes, a symbol of prosperity for the coming year. In addition, the round, golden shape of crêpes reminds people of the sun, evoking the return of spring after the dark and cold winter. It is also said that Pope Gelasius I ordered that crêpes be distributed to pilgrims arriving in Rome.

And if this video has made you hungry, all you have to do is practice making crêpes, thanks to the helpful videos.

results.title: Qui sont-ils ? Les Frères Bogdanoff
results.src_text:
Qui sont-ils ? Les Frères Bogdanoff  

En ce début d'année 2022, on apprend avec tristesse le décès d'Igor Bogdanoff, six jours seulement après celui de son frère Grichka. Mais qui étaient ces jumeaux au physique étrange que la France entière connaissait ?  

Igor et Grichka Bogdanoff faisaient partie du paysage médiatique français depuis plusieurs décennies. Ils se font connaître du grand public dans les années 80 lorsqu'ils co-présentent "Temps X" sur TF1, de 1979 à 1987, la toute première émission télévisée de science-fiction en France. Dans un décor de vaisseau spatial  et vêtus de combinaisons futuristes argentées, les jumeaux partagent leur passion pour la science et la science-fiction. Ils font notamment découvrir à un jeune public français  des séries cultes telles que Star Trek ou encore Docteur Who, tout en discutant de sujets scientifiques sérieux  et d'autres plus sensationnels comme les OVNIs et le voyage dans le temps.  

Dans les décennies qui suivent, les frères Bogdanoff publient plusieurs ouvrages scientifiques et autres ouvrages de vulgarisation scientifique qui rencontrent un vif succès auprès du public. Cependant, leurs thèses ainsi que la qualité de leur travail de vulgarisation leur attirent les foudres d'une partie de la communauté scientifique, qui en conteste la valeur scientifique dès les années 90.  

Dans les années 2000, les jumeaux font leur retour sur le petit écran  où ils présentent "Projet X 13" sur la chaîne 13ème Rue, puis l'émission "Rayons X" sous la forme d'avatars numériques sur France 2. Après 2010, ils se concentrent sur des activités de divertissement à la télévision et à la radio.  

Au fil des années, leur profonde transformation physique leur vaut de devenir un objet de fascination et de moquerie récurrent. Loin de s'en offusquer, ils en jouent eux-mêmes avec autodérision, en se qualifiant notamment d' "extraterrestres"  et en en entretenant le mystère jusqu'au bout. De par leurs personnalités excentriques et leurs physiques remarquables, les frères Bogdanoff sont devenus partie intégrante de la culture populaire française, où ils apparaissent régulièrement - sous forme de références, de caméos ou de parodies - dans la bande-dessinée, au cinéma ou encore dans la musique.
results.tgt_text:
Who were they? The Bogdanoff Brothers

At the beginning of 2022, we learned with sadness of the death of Igor Bogdanoff, just six days after that of his brother Grichka. But who were these twins with their unusual appearance that were known throughout France?

Igor and Grichka Bogdanoff had been part of the French media landscape for decades. They became well-known to the general public in the 1980s when they co-hosted "Temps X" on TF1, from 1979 to 1987, the first French television science fiction program. In a spaceship setting and wearing futuristic silver suits, the twins shared their passion for science and science fiction. They introduced a young French audience to cult series such as Star Trek and Doctor Who, while also discussing serious scientific topics and more sensational ones such as UFOs and time travel.

In the following decades, the Bogdanoff brothers published several scientific books and other popular science works, which were very successful with the public. However, their theories, as well as the quality of their popularization work, attracted the criticism of a portion of the scientific community, who began to question their scientific value as early as the 1990s.

In the 2000s, the twins returned to television, where they hosted "Project X 13" on the 13ème Rue channel, and then the show "Rayons X" in the form of digital avatars on France 2. After 2010, they focused on entertainment activities on television and radio.

Over the years, their profound physical transformation made them the subject of fascination and ridicule. Far from being offended, they played along with it, even self-deprecatingly, by referring to themselves as "extraterrestrials" and maintaining the mystery until the very end. Due to their eccentric personalities and remarkable appearances, the Bogdanoff brothers have become an integral part of French popular culture, where they regularly appear – in the form of references, cameos, or parodies – in comics, film, and music.

results.title: Ma première rentrée des classes
results.src_text:
Ma première rentrée des classes  

Je me souviens de mon premier jour d'école. J'avais trois ans et j'entrais à la maternelle. J'avais un joli cartable violet, une nouvelle jupe en jean et des chaussures roses à lacets. J'étais très fière, parce que j'allais enfin à l'école comme mes grands frères !  

En chemin, j'étais surexcitée et je courais presque à côté de Maman. Mais quand nous sommes arrivées près de l'école, il y avait beaucoup de monde, et j'ai commencé à être un peu nerveuse. J'ai attrapé la main de Maman et je me suis cachée derrière elle. Alors, elle s'est baissée et elle a chuchoté : "Tu sais, moi aussi, j'avais un peu peur à la rentrée des classes. Et puis, j'ai rencontré Tata Marina et elle est devenue ma meilleure copine."  

Soulagée, je suis sortie de ma cachette et nous sommes entrées dans la cour, la main dans la main. Je n'avais plus peur, et j'étais impatiente de rencontrer ma future meilleure amie !
results.tgt_text:
My First Day of School

I remember my first day of school. I was three years old and starting kindergarten. I had a pretty purple backpack, a new denim skirt, and pink shoes with laces. I was very proud, because I was finally going to school like my older brothers!

On the way, I was excited and almost running ahead of Mom. But when we got close to the school, there were a lot of people, and I started to feel a little nervous. I grabbed Mom's hand and hid behind her. Then, she knelt down and whispered, "You know, I was a little scared on my first day too. But then, I met Aunt Marina, and she became my best friend."

Feeling relieved, I came out from behind Mom, and we walked into the playground, holding hands. I wasn't scared anymore, and I was excited to meet my future best friend!
results.back_text:
Mon premier jour d'école

Je me souviens de mon premier jour d'école. J'avais trois ans et commençais la maternelle. J'avais un sac à dos violet, une jupe en jean neuve, et des chaussures roses avec des lacets. J'étais très fière, car j'allais enfin aller à l'école comme mes aînés !

En chemin, j'étais excitée et presque en train de courir devant Maman. Mais quand nous nous sommes approchées de l'école, il y avait beaucoup de monde, et j'ai commencé à me sentir un peu nerveuse. J'ai attrapé la main de Maman et je me suis cachée derrière elle. Ensuite, elle s'est agenouillée et m'a murmuré : "Tu sais, j'étais un peu effrayée le jour de mon premier. Mais ensuite, j'ai rencontré Tante Marina, et elle est devenue ma meilleure amie."

Soulagée, je suis sortie derrière Maman, et nous avons marché ensemble vers la cour de récréation, en nous tenant la main. Je n'avais plus peur, et j'étais impatiente de rencontrer ma future meilleure amie !

results.title: Charles Aznavour s'éteint à 94 ans
results.src_text:
La carrière de Charles Aznavour, décédé à l'âge de 94 ans  

"En haut de l'affiche", Charles Aznavour s'y était installé.  

Mes traits ont vieilli bien sûr  sous mon maquillage, mais la voix est là,  le geste est précis et j'ai du ressort.  

Charles Aznavour naît à Paris en 1924. Ses parents, arméniens, habitent un modeste appartement au 3e étage de cet immeuble, rue Monsieur Le Prince.  

"Bon, les lavabos, les water étaient à l'étage au-dessus. C[e n]'était pas tellement pratique, il faut bien le dire !"  

Ses premiers succès, il les obtient après la guerre, dans les années 40, en formant un duo avec le compositeur québécois Pierre Roche. Il est alors remarqué par Édith Piaf. Un succès qu'il doit à son infatigable envie et une bonne dose de discipline.  

"Il est professionnel comme il [n']est pas permis de l'être. C'est-à-dire qu'il n'y a pas un détail sur lequel il ne travaille pas d'arrache-pied, jusqu'à ce qu'il soit arrivé à la perfection."  

La perfection dans les compositions, mais aussi surtout dans les textes, comme il l'expliquait sur notre plateau il y a quelque temps.  

"La musique, c'est le support pour mes mots. D'autres vous diront - et ils auront raison parce que c'est leur manière de voir - vous diront : "Le mot accentue ma musique.". Ils mettent leur musique en premier. Moi, je mets les textes en premier."  

Sans savoir que coule en moi un flot de détresse.  

Ce flot de détresse, c'est la mémoire du génocide arménien. Amoureux de la langue française, il n'en oublie pas moins ses racines arméniennes, surtout après le tremblement de terre de 1995. À partir de 1995, il représente l'Arménie, dont il obtient la nationalité, dans plusieurs instances internationales, comme l'UNESCO ou l'ONU.  

Ses titres sont connus dans le monde entier. Disque d'or à plusieurs reprises au Royaume-Uni ou au Canada. En 1998, le magazine Time le sacre même chanteur de variétés le plus important du XXe siècle, devant Bob Dylan ou Frank Sinatra. En 2017, son nom est gravé sur le célèbre Walk of Fame de Los Angeles. Une vingtaine de Français seulement ont ce privilège.  

Affaibli suite à deux chutes au printemps 2018, Charles Aznavour est contraint d'annuler plusieurs dates de concert. Rétabli, quelques mois plus tard, il repart finalement en tournée mondiale : le Japon, l'Ukraine, la Belgique, puis la France. Lui qui se disait infatigable et rêvait d'un dernier concert d'adieux le 22 mai 2024 pour son 100e anniversaire, tire finalement sa révérence.  

Voici pour votre plus grand plaisir (et le nôtre !) quelques-unes des chansons inoubliables du "grand Charles".

results.title: Un dîner d'automne au restaurant
results.src_text:
Un dîner d'automne au restaurant  

- Bonsoir, suivez-moi s'il vous plaît ! Vous pouvez vous installer à cette table, à côté du comptoir. Voici le menu.  

- Merci ! Peut-on avoir une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît ?  

- Bien sûr ! Voici deux verres et un pichet d'eau fraîche.  

- Merci ! Mmm, ça a l'air appétissant ! Que nous recommandez-vous ?  

- Le plat du jour est très populaire : une saucisse de Toulouse avec un gratin de pommes de terre. Et le chef prépare aussi un excellent boeuf bourguignon. Je vous laisse un moment pour décider…  

- Vous avez fait votre choix ?  

- Oui, je voudrais la formule à vingt euros, avec une soupe au potiron et le risotto aux champignons.  

- Et en dessert ? Je vous recommande la glace aux marrons.  

- Merci, mais je préfère la mousse au chocolat, s'il vous plaît.  

- Très bon choix Monsieur ! Et vous, Madame ?  

- Je vais juste prendre la quiche aux oignons et au fromage de chèvre parce que je n'ai pas très faim. Est-ce que je peux avoir une salade aussi ?  

- Tout à fait ! Et pour boire ?  

- Moi, je voudrais un verre de vin rouge, un bordeaux si possible.  

- Oui, très bien ! Et vous Madame, désirez-vous un verre de vin ?  

- Non, merci ! Une tasse de thé s'il vous plaît.  

- Parfait ! Je reviens dans un instant avec vos boissons !
results.tgt_text:
Dinner in an autumn restaurant

- Good evening, please follow me! You can sit at this table, next to the counter. Here is the menu.

- Thank you! Could we have a carafe of water, please?

- Of course! Here are two glasses and a carafe of fresh water.

- Thank you! Mmm, that looks delicious! What would you recommend?

- The dish of the day is very popular: Toulouse sausage with potato gratin. And the chef is also preparing an excellent beef bourguignon. I'll leave you some time to decide…

- Have you made your choice?

- Yes, I would like the twenty euro set menu, with pumpkin soup and mushroom risotto.

- And for dessert? I recommend the chestnut ice cream.

- Thank you, but I would prefer the chocolate mousse, please.

- Excellent choice, sir! And you, madam?

- I'll just have the onion and goat cheese quiche because I'm not very hungry. Can I also have a salad?

- Certainly! And to drink?

- I would like a glass of red wine, preferably a Bordeaux.

- Yes, very good! And you, madam, would you like a glass of wine?

- No, thank you! Just a cup of tea, please.

- Perfect! I'll be back shortly with your drinks!

Prévisions Météo (du 4 au 6 octobre 2017)  

Mesdames, Messieurs, bonjour. Pour cette après-midi, grâce aux conditions anticycloniques qui s'affirment par l'ouest du pays, le temps reste calme et bien ensoleillé, avec quand même quelques passages nuageux qui seront un petit peu plus nombreux  entre le Cotentin et près des frontières nord. En revanche, on verra un plein soleil qui va de nouveau s'imposer le long de la façade atlantique ainsi que vers le Golfe du Lion et jusqu'au niveau des régions centrales. Et côté températures, elles sont globalement stationnaires par rapport à hier, avec des valeurs qui sont de saison, ou parfois un peu justes sur la moitié nord. On conserve toujours une certaine douceur dans les régions plus au sud, mais on a quand même perdu quelques degrés par rapport à hier - notamment autour de 3 à 4 degrés vers le Languedoc-Roussillon - et on remonte quand même jusqu'à 25 degrés vers la Corse.  

Pour jeudi, changement radical : une perturbation bien active progresse sur les régions plus au nord, elle donne des pluies régulières entre le Bassin parisien  ainsi que près des frontières nord. Elle s'accompagne de vent. Les pluies sont beaucoup plus faibles du côté de la Bretagne. Cette perturbation va rapidement progresser vers les régions de l'est, et rapidement, l'air froid, plus sec, et les belles éclaircies vont également progresser sur les régions plus au nord. Plus au sud, on va conserver un temps calme et un très beau soleil. Les températures après cette fraîcheur matinale seront donc tout naturellement contrastées en journée, avec des valeurs qui seront parfois un peu justes pour la saison sur la moitié nord, mais au contraire une belle douceur qui va se maintenir sur la moitié sud, avec même des pointes attendues autour de 28, voire même 30 degrés dans le Languedoc-Roussillon.  

Et pour je...vendredi, là encore gros changement, puisque les températures sont en nette baisse dans cette traîne de nord-ouest, l'air froid progresse. Au nord comme au sud, les valeurs sont toutes inférieures aux normales, de 3 à 5 degrés en moyenne, cette traîne sera néanmoins un petit peu plus active le long des frontières de l'est avec un ciel plus nuageux, mais également quelques averses possibles. On note d'ailleurs la présence de quelques flocons dès 1.600 mètres. Et sur le pourtour méditerranéen, c'est le soleil qui s'impose, mais au prix d'un mistral et d'une tramontane atteignant jusqu'à 90 voire 100 km/heure.  

Je vous souhaite une excellente après-midi, et je vous dis à très bientôt !

Weather Forecast (October 4-6, 2017)

Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. For this afternoon, thanks to the stable weather conditions brought by the anticyclone over the western part of the country, the weather will remain calm and sunny, with some cloud cover, particularly between the Cotentin and near the northern borders. However, we will see plenty of sunshine along the Atlantic coast, as well as towards the Gulf of Lion and up to the central regions. And in terms of temperatures, they are generally stable compared to yesterday, with values that are typical for the season, or slightly lower in the northern half. We still have a certain warmth in the southern regions, but we have lost a few degrees compared to yesterday – particularly around 3 to 4 degrees in the Languedoc-Roussillon region – and we are still reaching 25 degrees in Corsica.

For Thursday, a significant change: an active weather system is moving into the northern regions, bringing regular rainfall between the Paris Basin and near the northern borders. It is accompanied by wind. Rainfall is much weaker in Brittany. This weather system will quickly move towards the eastern regions, and the cold, dry air and clear skies will also move into the northern regions. In the south, we will maintain calm weather and very sunny conditions. Therefore, the temperatures after this morning's coolness will be noticeably different during the day, with values that are sometimes slightly lower than average in the northern half, but a pleasant warmth will continue in the southern half, with temperatures potentially reaching 28, or even 30 degrees in the Languedoc-Roussillon region.

And for Friday, another significant change: the temperatures are falling sharply in this northwestern area, with cold air moving in. Across the north and south, the values are all below the average, by 3 to 5 degrees on average. This northwestern area will be a little more active along the eastern borders with cloudier skies, but also some possible showers. We can also note the presence of some snowflakes from 1,600 meters. And along the Mediterranean coast, it is the sun that prevails, but at the cost of a strong mistral and tramontane winds reaching up to 90 or 100 km/h.

I wish you a pleasant afternoon, and I will see you soon!

results.src_text:
S'occuper sans écran - La drôle d’humeur de Marina Rollman  

D'abord, voici Marina Rollman !  

Merci les amis ! Alors, qu'est-ce que j'ai fait moi ce weekend ? Eh ben, j'ai... Oh là là ! C'est des applaudissements complètement fous ! Moi, qu'est-ce que j'ai fait ce weekend les amis ? J'ai éteint mon téléphone et mon ordinateur parce que j'en avais marre, voilà. Je sentais qu'ils avaient pris le pouvoir. Ben ouais, parce qu'on croit toujours que le soulèvement des machines, c'est un truc du futur, mais pas du tout en fait. Moi, la semaine passée, je me suis coupée parce que j'étais en train de cuisiner en regardant une émission de cuisine ! C'est-à-dire qu'eux, ils étaient en train de faire  des ballottines de tarama sur une émulsion de yuzu, là; moi, j'étais en train de gérer une espuma de coquillettes sur son beurre de... beurre, bref, et tu regardes l'écran, tu te coupes. T'imagines le niveau d'amour qu'on a pour les écrans. Je les aime tellement que  je suis d'accord de ne pas regarder mes doigts alors qu'il y a un couteau à côté !  

C'est pareil pour les piétons qui se prennent des vélos parce qu'ils ont leurs écouteurs, ou les gens qui envoient des SMS en conduisant, tu vois. En fait, la domination des machines, c'est pas du tout un truc épique. [Tu] sais, le soulèvement de l'intelligence artificielle, c'est pas un truc excitant à la "Matrix". C'est un petit despotisme humiliant au quotidien, comme ça, elles nous remettent à notre place très subtilement. Elles font genre :  "Franchement, tu m'éteins quand tu veux, hein. C'est un gros bouton, c'est facile, en plus il y [n']en a pas beaucoup. Sinon, je suis tout petit, tu peux me mettre dans ta poche si tu veux, ou tu peux me laisser me décharger, vraiment, c'est toi qui gères..." En fait, rien du tout ! Tu fais une crise d'angoisse parce que tu [ne] trouves plus ton chargeur.  

Et donc, bref, il a fallu s'occuper sans écran les amis. Alors, heureusement, on a plein de jeux avec mon mari en ces temps de sous-activité. Par exemple, on a le jeu du café. Je ne sais pas si vous connaissez. Alors, le jeu du café, la règle c'est : [il] y a un des deux joueurs qui dit : "Je fais du café, t[u]'en veux ?". Et là, on attend. Et si l'autre joueur, il dit : "Ouais, je veux bien.", eh ben, on lui fait du café, voilà. C'est un jeu où personne ne perd ! C'est le jeu pour les gens qui étaient choisis en dernier quand il fallait faire des équipes pour le ballon-prisonnier, tu vois. Alors, ça [ne] fait pas des compétiteurs coriaces, mais c'est plus pour former les gens qui vont travailler à l'ONU, tu vois. Mais c'est bon enfant, voilà.  

L'autre jeu marrant qu'on a en ce moment, c'est le jeu du "Ça va pas ?". Alors, c'est très simple, là aussi, [il] y a un joueur qui demande à l'autre si "ça va pas ?", et alors, normalement, le jeu part tout de suite. Normalement, ça va très vite, l'autre joueur, il relance : "Pourquoi ça va pas ? J[e n]'ai pas l'air ? Tu crois que je suis malade ? Pourquoi tu veux toujours savoir ce que je pense ? Putain, mais j'ai l'impression qu'[il n']y a rien qui va en fait !" Ça peut partir très vite. Ce qui est pratique avec le jeu du "ça va pas", c'est qu'on peut aussi jouer tout seul, voilà, on peut se faire des petites astuces à soi-même.  

Après, là où ça se complexifie, le jeu du "ça va pas",  c'est si on a un joueur aguerri en face qui emploie la tactique dite de la "désescalade". Et qui, à "ça va pas", répond :  "Moi, ça va super, Amour. Ça te va bien ce pull. Je suis content d'être là avec toi.". Alors, si c'est le cas, si vous jouez avec des joueurs expérimentés, il faut rentrer dans une deuxième phase du jeu, un peu plus offensive, qui consiste, peu importe la réponse, à répéter le "Ça va pas ?", éventuellement accompagné d'un "T'es sûr ? Parce que je te connais un peu quand même, hein", une fois par heure, à peu près.  

Idéalement, vous ajoutez quelques verres de vin ou un coup de fil un peu contrariant à un proche pour attiser un peu les enjeux. Et si tu fais ça sur une journée, normalement, en début de soirée, on a une partie qui peut vraiment se révéler très chouette, hein. "Ça va pas ?" "Quoi, ça va pas ? Tu veux me contrôler, c'est ça que tu veux ? C'est moi qui vais pas ? C'est toi qui vas pas avec ton vieux pull, là !" Et là, on est sûr de passer une soirée divertissante, du fun pour toute la famille, un vrai moment de partage, loin des écrans, et de toute la violence que nous impose internet. Voilà, finalement, c'est ça.

"Screen-Free Fun - Marina Rollman's Quirky Take"

First, here's Marina Rollman!

Thanks, everyone! So, what did I do this weekend? Well, I... Oh my! That's quite the reaction! What did I do this weekend, everyone? I turned off my phone and computer because I was tired of it. I felt like they were taking over. Well, yeah, we always think that the rise of machines is something from the future, but it's actually happening right now. Last week, I almost got into an accident because I was cooking while watching a cooking show! I mean, I was making a tarama ball with a yuzu emulsion, and they were making something else entirely. It's like, you're focused on your food, and then you look up, and you realize you're completely out of touch. It's amazing how much we rely on screens. I'm so used to them that I'd rather not see my fingers while I'm using a knife!

The same thing happens with pedestrians who get hit by bikes because they're listening to music, or people who text while driving. In reality, the rise of machines isn't some epic, sci-fi event. You know, the rise of artificial intelligence isn't like in "The Matrix." It's a subtle, everyday form of control. It's like they're saying, "Honestly, you can turn me off whenever you want. It's a simple button, and there are plenty of them. Or, I'm small and unobtrusive, you can put me in your pocket, or you can just let me charge. It's up to you..." Basically, it's not a big deal. You just have a minor anxiety attack because you can't find your charger.

So, basically, we had to find ways to have fun without screens. Luckily, we have a lot of games to play with my husband. For example, we have a game called "Coffee." I don't know if you're familiar with it. The game is simple: one person says, "Do you want some coffee?" And then, you wait. If the other person says, "Yes, I'd like some," then you make them coffee. results.src_text:
Soirée d'Halloween à Pfaffenhoffen en Alsace 

JOURNALISTE 1: Mille deux cents personnes venues trembler de peur, la soirée d'Halloween hier à Pfaffenhoffen a fait un carton. À l'origine, un jeune décorateur amateur  qui a transformé le garage automobile de la ville en maison hantée. Les visiteurs ont dû survivre à un parcours semé d'embûches et de monstres en tous genres pour obtenir des bonbons. Frissons et succès garantis !  

Le reportage de Marie Coulon et Emmanuel Gambette :  

JOURNALISTE 2: C'est le genre d'endroit  dans lequel vous n'avez pas vraiment envie d'entrer, parce qu'une fois à l'intérieur... vos nerfs sont mis à rude épreuve. Les mécaniciens du garage ont fini comme ça, pendus à des crochets. Devenus mort-vivants, ils veulent transformer les visiteurs  en barquettes de viande. Un peu "gore", d'accord, mais frissons garantis.  

C'est comment ?  

VISITEUSE: Très bien. Ça fait peur !  

VISITEUSE 2: Oh, ça fait peur, hein, ça fait peur, mais même les grands, ils ont peur !  

JOURNALISTE 2: Au total, 400 mètres carrés de parcours semé d'embûches. Le projet fou d'un jeune artiste de 28 ans originaire de Pfaffenhoffen.  

ARTISTE: Non, c'est vraiment le moment où je peux me faire le plus plaisir en art, euh, c'est là où on se défoule  et on va au-delà de nos limites, et on profite comme aujourd'hui vraiment d'un espace pour faire encore plus grand, toujours plus grand que ce qu'on a déjà fait.  

JOURNALISTE 2: Jean-Christophe Matz a déboursé mille euros sur ses fonds propres et mobilisé plusieurs entreprises locales  pour réaliser en seulement deux mois ce garage hanté. Avec l'aide aussi d'une bande de copains un peu mal en point ! Leur but : offrir un vrai spectacle aux petits comme aux grands.  

FILLETTE: Les acteurs, ils mettaient bien en scène, ça faisait super peur.  

VISITEUSE: Les décors sont supers, vraiment c'est bluffant ! Les squelettes, et puis les maquillages, euh, enfin c'est vraiment, vraiment magnifique ! À faire peur !  

JOURNALISTE 2: Et pour avoir failli mourir de peur, une petite récompense tout de même !  

FEMME: Vous venez d'où ? Vous êtes combien ?  

JOURNALISTE 2: Au total, près de 1 200 courageux sont venus de toute l'Alsace pour participer à cette nuit de l'horreur.  

JOURNALISTE 1: Et c'est la fin de ce flash d'information, merci de l'avoir suivi. L'info continue...
